name: Levels of Processing Effect
description: Information processed for meaning is remembered better later than information processed only for shallow surface features. The way something is encoded matters at least as much as how often it was merely seen.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to onboarding, training, educational products, reflective prompts, and any experience meant to be remembered later. It has much weaker direct value for routine efficiency-oriented UI decisions where recognition, not retention, is the main goal.
prevalence_note: Common in learning science, education, and training design, but not a mainstream named law in general product UX critique.

findings.description: A PET neuroimaging study replicated the behavioral levels-of-processing effect (better recognition memory for semantically vs. perceptually encoded nouns) and identified its neural correlate: significantly greater left inferior prefrontal cortex activation during semantic encoding than perceptual encoding. Independently confirms the original 1975 behavioral finding via a completely different method (neuroimaging), by an overlapping author team including the entry's original researchers (Craik, Tulving), and adds a real neural mechanism this corpus didn't previously have.
findings.source_title: Neuroanatomical correlates of encoding in episodic memory: levels of processing effect.
findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

findings.description: Words processed semantically and more deeply were remembered substantially better later than words processed only for shallow perceptual features, the canonical levels-of-processing effect in episodic memory.
findings.source_title: Depth of processing and the retention of words in episodic memory.
